sections.description: The video shows belts with wear signs such as rough surfaces, rust staining, and sections that look worn smooth. Squealing when starting the car is highlighted as an indicator of belt wear, especially with a manual tensioner where slack is not automatically taken up.
sections.title: Observations and symptoms of belt wear

concepts: Cracks and dry rot in rubber
sections.description: Detailed criteria for judging belt health are presented: cracks, dry rot, fraying, hard and inflexible belts, and worn grooves. The presenter contrasts the degraded belt with a new, flexible belt to illustrate what healthy belt performance looks like.
sections.title: Wear indicators and belt condition criteria

sections.description: The worn belts are replaced with new belts, and the presenter notes that the embarrassing squeal is gone after replacement, concluding the inspection and replacement process.
sections.title: Replacement outcome and conclusion

summary: The video from 1A Auto demonstrates inspecting two dry drive belts on a vehicle that uses manual tensioners (no auto tensioner). The presenter notes squealing on startup as belts wear, identifies wear indicators such as cracks, fraying, and stiffness, and compares worn belts to a new belt. He explains that automatic tensioners can mask wear, whereas manual tensioners allow wear to show as slipping and noise. The lesson concludes with replacing the belts and removing the squeal. The guidance emphasizes visual and tactile belt checks and replacing worn belts rather than attempting to retension them.
title: Inspecting and Replacing Dry Drive Belts with Manual Tensioners
